div.head: MEMB. 4. SUBSECT. 1.
Prognostics of Love-Melancholy.
div.p: What Fires, Torments, Cares, Jealousies, Suspicions, Fears, Griefs, Anxieties, accompany such as are in love, I have sufficiently said: the next question is what will be the event of such miseries, what they foretell. Some are of opinion that this love cannot be cured, Nullis amor est medicabilis herbis [love cannot be healed by any herb], it accompanies them to the Semper moritur, nunquam mortuus est qui amat [He who loves is always dying but never dead]. Aen Silv.last,

l.hi: Idem amor exitio est pecori pecorisque magistro,

lg.l: [The same love is the ruin of the herd and the herd’s master,]

div.p: and is so continuate, that by no persuasion almost it may be relieved. Bid me not love, said Euryal. ep. ad Lucretiam, apud Aeneam Silvium.Euryalus, bid the Mountains come down into the plains, bid the Rivers run back to their fountains; I can as soon leave to love, as the Sun leave his course;

l.hi: Et prius aequoribus pisces, & montibus umbrae,
Et volucres deerunt sylvis, & murmura ventis,

lg.l: Quam mihi discedent formosae Amaryllidis ignes.
First Seas shall want their Fish, the mountains shade,
Woods singing birds, the wind’s murmur shall fade,
Than my fair Amaryllis’ love allayed.

div.p: Bid me not love, bid a deaf man hear, a blind man see, a dumb speak, lame run, counsel can do no good, a sick man cannot relish, no Physic can ease me.

lg.l: Non prosunt domino quae prosunt omnibus artes.
[The arts that help everyone don’t help their master.]

div.p: As Apollo confessed, and Jupiter himself could not be cured.

lg.l: Solus amor morbi non habet artificem.
Physic can soon cure every disease,
Est orcus ille, vis est immedicabilis, est rabies insana [It is a hell, an incurable compulsion, a raving madness].Excepting love, that can it not appease.

div.p: But whether Love may be cured or no, and by what means, shall be explained in his place; in the meantime, if it take his course, and be not otherwise eased or amended, it breaks out into outrageous often and prodigious events. Amor & Liber violenti dii sunt, as Lib. 2.Tatius observes, & eo usque animum incendunt, ut pudoris oblivisci cogant, Love and Bacchus are so violent Gods, so furiously rage in our minds, that they make us forget all honesty, shame and common civility. For such men ordinarily as are thoroughly possessed with this humour, become insensati & insani [irrational and insane], for it is Virg. Ecl. 3.amor insanus [insane love], as the Poet calls it, beside themselves, and as I have proved, no better than beasts, irrational, stupid, headstrong, void of fear of God or men, they frequently forswear themselves, spend, steal, commit incests, rapes, adulteries, murders, depopulate Towns, Cities, Countries, to satisfy their lust.

lg.l: R. T.A Devil ’tis, and mischief such doth work,
As never yet did Pagan, Jew, or Turk.

div.p: The wars of Troy may be a sufficient witness; and as Appian lib. 5 hist. saith of Antony and Cleopatra, their Love brought themselves, and all Egypt into extreme and miserable calamities. The end of her is as bitter as wormwood, and as sharp as a two-edged sword, Prov. 5. 4, 5, Her feet go down to death, her steps lead on to hell. She is more bitter than death (Eccles. 7. 28) and the sinner shall be taken by her.

lg.l: Plautus.Qui in amore praecipitavit, pejus perit, quam qui saxo salit.

div.p: Ut corpus pondere, sic animus amore praecipitatur [As the body by its weight, so the soul is cast down by love]. Austin 2 de civ. dei, cap. 28.He that runs headlong from the top of a rock, is not so bad a case, as he that falls into this gulf of love. For hence, saith Dial.Platina, comes Repentance, Desperation, Dotage, they lose themselves, their wits, and make shipwreck of their fortunes altogether: madness, to make away themselves and others, violent death. Prognosticatio est talis, saith Gordonius, Idem Savonarola, & plures alii, &c. [Savonarola says the same, and many others, etc.] Rabidam facturus Orexin [To produce a fierce appetite]. Juven.si non succurratur iis, aut in maniam cadunt, aut moriuntur, the prognostication is, [if they aren’t helped] they will either run mad, or die. For if this passion continue, saith Cap. de Heroico Amore.Aelian Montaltus, it makes the blood hot, thick, and black; and if the inflammation get into the brain, with continual meditation and waking, it so dries it up, that madness follows, or else they make away themselves,

lg.l: Virg. Ecl. 2.O Coridon, Coridon, quae te dementia cepit?
[O Corydon, Corydon, what insanity has seized you?]

div.p: Now as Arnaldus adds, it will speedily work these effects, if it be not presently helped; Insani fiunt aut sibi ipsis desperantes mortem afferunt. Languentes cito mortem aut maniam patiuntur [They become insane, or kill themselves in despair. Languishing, they quickly suffer death or mania].They will pine away, run mad, and die upon a sudden; facile incidunt in maniam, saith Valescus, quickly mad, nisi succurratur, if good order be not taken,

l.hi: Eheu triste jugum quisquis amoris habet,

lg.l: Is prius ac norit se periisse perit.
Oh heavy yoke of love, which whoso bears,
Is quite undone, and that at unawares.

div.p: So she confessed of herself in the Poet.

lg.l: ——— Theocritus Idyl. 14.Insaniam priusquam quis sentiat,
Vix pili intervallo a furore absum.
I shall be mad before it be perceived,
An hairbreadth off scarce am I, now distracted.

div.p: As mad as Orlando for his Angelica, or Hercules for his Hylas,

l.hi: At ille ruebat quo pedes ducebant, furibundus,
Nam illi saevus Deus intus jecur laniabat,

lg.l: He went he car’d not whither, mad he was,
The cruel God so tortur’d him, alas.

div.p: At the sight of Hero I cannot tell how many ran Lucian Imag. So for Lucian’s Mistress all that saw her, and could not enjoy her, ran mad, or hanged themselves.mad,

lg.l: Musaeus.Alius vulnus celans insanit pulchritudine puellae.
And whilst he doth conceal his grief,
Madness comes on him like a thief.

div.p: Go to Bedlam for examples. It is so well known in every village, how many have either died for love, or voluntarily made away themselves, that I need not much labour to prove it; Ovid. met. 10.Nec modus aut requies nisi mors reperitur amoris [no end or rest can be found for love but death]: death is the common Catastrophe to such persons.

l.hi: Mori mihi contingat, non enim alia

lg.l: Liberatio ab aerumnis fuerit ullo pacto istis.
Would I were dead, for naught God knows,
But death can rid me of these woes.

div.p: Aeneas Silvius.As soon as Euryalus departed from Siena, Lucretia his Paramour never looked up, no jests could exhilarate her sad mind, no joys comfort her wounded and distressed soul, but a little after she fell sick and died. But this is a gentle end, a natural death, such persons commonly make away themselves:

lg.l: ——— proprioque in sanguine laetus,

l.hi: Indignantem animam vacuas effudit in auras;

lg.l: [… delighting in his own blood,
He released his scornful soul into the clear air;]

l.hi: Sed moriamur ait, sic sic juvat ire per umbras;

lg.l: [‘But let me die,’ she said. ‘Thus, thus I gladly go into the shadows’;]

div.p: Pyramus and Thisbe, Medea, Pausanias Achaicis lib. 7.Coresus and Callirhoe, Megarensis amore flagrans [Blazing with love for a Megaran girl]. Lucian Tom. 4.Theagenes the Philosopher and many Myriads besides, and so will ever do,

lg.l: ——— Ovid. 3 Met.& mihi fortis

l.hi: Est manus, est & amor, dabit hic in vulnera vires,

lg.l: [… and I have a firm
Hand, and I, too, love; this will give power to the blows,]
Who ever heard a story of more woe,
Than that of Juliet and her Romeo?

div.p: Read Parthenium in Eroticis, and Plutarch’s amatorias narrationes or love stories, all tending almost to this purpose. Valleriola lib. 2 observ. 7 hath a lamentable narration of a Merchant his patient, Furibundus putavit se videre Imaginem puellae, & coram loqui blandiens illi, &c. [In a frenzy, he thought he saw an apparition of the girl, and that he was fawning on her and talking in her presence, etc.]that raving through impatience of love, had he not been watched, would every while have offered violence to himself. Amatus Lusitanus cent. 3 cur. 56 hath such Juven. Hebraeus [A Jewish youth].another story, and Felix Plater. med. observ. lib. 1 a third of a young Gentleman that studied Physic, and for the love of a Doctor’s daughter, having no hope to compass his desire, poisoned himself. Gotardus Arthus Gallobelgicus, nund. vernal. 1615. Collum novacula aperuit: & inde expiravit [He slit his neck with a knife and then expired].Anno 1615, a barber in Frankfurt, because his wench was betrothed to another, cut his own throat. At Neuberg the same year a young man, because he could not get her Parents’ consent, killed his sweetheart, and afterward himself, desiring this of the magistrate, as he gave up the Ghost, that they might be buried in one grave,

l.hi: Quodque rogis superest una requiescat in urna,

lg.l: [And that whatever remains from the funeral pyres should rest in a single urn,]

div.p: which Boccace.Gismunda besought of Tancredus her father, that she might be in like sort buried with Guiscardus her lover, that so their bodies might lie together in the grave, as their souls wander about Sedes eorum qui pro amoris impatientia pereunt [The home of those who perish from being unable to bear love]. Virg. 6 Aeneid.Campos lugentes [the Fields of Mourning] in the Elysian fields,

lg.l: ——— quos durus amor crudeli tabe peredit,
[… {where} those whom harsh love devours with cruel decay,]
——— & myrtea circum
Sylva tegit: curae non ipsa in morte relinquunt.
[… and a myrtle grove encircles them:
Even in death, their cares do not leave them.]

div.p: You have not yet heard the worst, they do not offer violence to themselves in this rage of lust but unto others, their nearest and dearest friends. Sal. Val. Max.Catiline killed his only son, misitque ad orci pallida, lethi obnubila, obsita tenebris loca [and dispatched him to the pallid underworld, the darkened place of death, the land covered by shadows], for the love of Aurelia Orestilla, quod ejus nuptias vivo filio recusaret [because she refused to marry him with his son alive]. Sabel. lib. 3 En. 6.Laodice the sister of Mithridates, poisoned her husband, to give content to a base fellow whom she loved. Curtius lib. 5.Alexander to please Thais a concubine of his, set Persepolis on fire. Chalcocondilas de reb. Turcicis lib. 9.Nerius’ wife, a widow and Lady of Athens, for the love of a Venetian Gentleman, betrayed the City; and he for her sake, murdered his wife, the daughter of a Nobleman in Venice. Nicephorus Greg. hist. lib. 8.Constantine Despota, made away Catharine his wife, turned his son Michael and his other children out of doors, for the love of a base Scrivener’s daughter in Thessalonica, with whose beauty he was enamoured. Parthenius Erot. lib. cap. 5.Leucophrye betrayed the City where she dwelt, for her sweetheart’s sake, that was in the enemy’s Camp. Idem cap. 21.Pisidice the Governor’s daughter of Methymna for the love of Achilles, betrayed the whole Island to him, her father’s enemy. Idem cap. 9.Diognetus did as much in the City where he dwelt, for the love of Polycrita. Medea for the love of Jason, taught him how to tame the fire-breathing brass-feeted Bulls, and kill the mighty dragon that kept the golden fleece, and tore her little brother Absyrtus in pieces, that her father Aeetes, might have something to detain him, while she ran away with her beloved Jason, &c. Such Acts and Scenes hath this Tragicomedy of love.
